To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the sensitivity to CP violation is excellent for all setups, with the exception of the liquid scinitillator detector at 130 km, and that the sensitivity to the mass hierarchy is good for all setups, except the liquid scintillating detector at 130, 230 and 1300 km.

a liquid argont or water \v Cerenkov detector can discover CP violation at the $3\sigma $ CL for $60%- 70%$ of all possible values of $\delta$ and $\theta_{13},$ and that a $3\sigam$ determination of the sign of $\Delta m_{32}^{2}$ is possible for almost all setups at baselines larger than 650 km.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the physics potential of the LAGUNAs, which is a European design study for a large underground facility.
the impact of the Daya Bay and REON results on the physics potential of long baseline experiments, with a special focus on the European LAGUNA project.
the physics potential of a long baseline neutrino oscillation experiment in the context of the LAGUNAs project.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the physics reach of a superbeam with a megaton-scale detector in a LAGUNA location would be sufficient to make a $3 \sigma$ discovery for the CP-violating parameter $\delta_{\rm CP}$ and to determine the mass hierarchy for the majority of the parameter space, for any baseline between 130 km and 2300 km, and for any of the three detector technologies considered.

the physics reach of a European long-baseline neutrino beam is very promising for all three detector technologies under consideration, with the exception of the liquid scinitillator detector at 130 km.

a liquid scintillator or liquid argon detector can make a discovery of CP violation at the $3\sigma $CL for $70\%$ of the possible values of the CP phase $\delta$, while a water \v{ C}erenkov detector is capable of doing so for $90\%$.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in the context of a long-baseline superbeam experiment with the CERN neutrino beam, a liquid argon detector is the most promising option, with a liquid scintillator or water \v Cerenkov detector at second and third places respectively.

the physics reach of long-baseline superbeams with $\theta_{13}\gtrsim 9^\circ$ is excellent, with a liquid argon detector being slightly better than a water \v{ C}erenkov detector and the liquid scintillators detector being less sensitive to CP-violation.

a liquid argont detector at 130 km or at 2300 km is a better option for a CERN neutrino beam than the water \v{ C}erenkov detector at 130 or 2300 km, and the water \v Cerenkov detector at Gran Sasso is a better option than the liquid argon or liquid scintillator detectors.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a European megaton-scale detector can make a discovery of leptonic CP violation and determine the mass hierarchy for any baseline between 130 and 2300 km and for a wide range of beam parameters and detector performances.

a European neutrino facility can provide a unique opportunity to study neutrino oscillations in a wide range of parameters, with an excellent sensitivity to CP-violating effects and the neutrino mass hierarchy.
the physics reach of long-baseline neutrino oscillation setups can be greatly affected by the value of $\theta_{3}$, which is currently being determined.
